questions.question: In the context of LLM inference, which statement best distinguishes throughput from latency?
questions.choice_A: Throughput measures tokens processed per second, while latency measures the time to produce a token or response.
questions.choice_B: Throughput measures how long a single request takes, while latency measures how many requests can be served per second.
questions.choice_C: Throughput measures average batch size, while latency measures maximum memory usage.
questions.choice_D: Throughput and latency are the same when batch size is one.

questions.question: When designing a benchmarking setup for LLMs, why is it important to report sequence length and batch size explicitly?
questions.choice_A: They are only relevant for training, not inference.
questions.choice_B: They strongly influence both memory footprint and the token generation rate, making results otherwise non-comparable.
questions.choice_C: They only affect latency, not throughput.
questions.choice_D: They have negligible impact if the model uses caching.

questions.question: What is a common pitfall when measuring per-token latency during autoregressive generation?
questions.choice_A: Using too long a context window.
questions.choice_B: Measuring on CPU instead of GPU.
questions.choice_C: Averaging over all tokens without separating first-token latency from steady-state token latency.
questions.choice_D: Using a fixed random seed.

questions.question: Which approach best captures end-to-end energy consumption of an LLM inference workload?
questions.choice_A: Counting only multiply-accumulate operations (MACs) from the model’s FLOP estimate.
questions.choice_B: Estimating energy by multiplying FLOPs by an assumed joules-per-FLOP constant.
questions.choice_C: Using a simulator that ignores memory transfers and I/O overheads.
questions.choice_D: Measuring wall-plug power with a power meter over the entire run and integrating to get joules.

questions.question: Why is it necessary to specify hardware configuration (e.g., GPU model, interconnect, CPU) in performance reports?
questions.choice_A: Hardware characteristics determine compute, memory bandwidth, and communication limits that shape throughput, latency, and energy.
questions.choice_B: To comply with licensing requirements for benchmarks.
questions.choice_C: Because software frameworks cannot influence performance once hardware is fixed.
questions.choice_D: To avoid having to report batch size and sequence length.

questions.question: How does batch size typically affect throughput and latency in LLM inference on GPUs?
questions.choice_A: Increasing batch size decreases both throughput and latency.
questions.choice_B: Increasing batch size usually increases throughput but can increase per-request latency due to queueing and larger kernels.
questions.choice_C: Batch size only impacts memory and has no effect on throughput.
questions.choice_D: Batch size effects disappear when using model parallelism.

questions.question: What is the main reason to separate parameter, activation, and KV-cache memory when reporting memory footprint?
questions.choice_A: They are stored in different file formats.
questions.choice_B: Only parameter memory is relevant at inference time.
questions.choice_C: They scale differently with sequence length and batch size, influencing capacity planning and scalability analysis.
questions.choice_D: Activation memory is unpredictable and should be ignored.

questions.question: When using pipeline parallelism during measurement, which artifact most commonly biases latency results if unaccounted for?
questions.choice_A: Stronger regularization during inference.
questions.choice_B: Reduced precision arithmetic.
questions.choice_C: Tokenization inconsistencies.
questions.choice_D: Pipeline bubbles and microbatching overheads that inflate end-to-end latency for short sequences.

questions.question: Which normalization makes cross-precision comparisons most interpretable for energy and performance?
questions.choice_A: Reporting tokens/sec and joules/token for each precision under identical batch size, sequence length, and hardware.
questions.choice_B: Reporting only wall-clock time regardless of batch size.
questions.choice_C: Reporting relative speedups without listing the baseline precision.
questions.choice_D: Reporting GPU utilization percentage only.

questions.question: Why should warm-up iterations be included before timing inference kernels on GPUs?
questions.choice_A: To reduce numerical error.
questions.choice_B: To amortize one-time costs like CUDA context initialization, kernel caching, and data layout setup so steady-state performance is measured.
questions.choice_C: To ensure deterministic token outputs.
questions.choice_D: To better estimate peak memory bandwidth by overfilling caches.

questions.question: Which statement about arithmetic-only energy estimates is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: They typically overestimate energy because they ignore memory costs.
questions.choice_B: They are sufficient for cross-hardware comparisons without caveats.
questions.choice_C: They can mislead because memory traffic, control overheads, and idling can dominate energy in real workloads.
questions.choice_D: They are equivalent to end-to-end power measurements if FLOP counts are precise.

questions.question: When comparing two implementations (e.g., baseline attention vs. FlashAttention), what is the most rigorous way to attribute performance differences?
questions.choice_A: Swap both the model and tokenizer to the latest versions.
questions.choice_B: Change batch size to maximize each implementation’s throughput independently.
questions.choice_C: Use different GPUs to isolate compute-bound behavior.
questions.choice_D: Hold model, precision, hardware, batch size, and sequence length fixed; swap only the attention kernel and measure throughput, latency, memory, and energy.

questions.question: What is the best practice for reporting latency in an autoregressive decoder?
questions.choice_A: Report only average end-to-end time per request.
questions.choice_B: Report only time-to-first-token (TTFT).
questions.choice_C: Report TTFT and steady-state per-token latency separately, as they reflect different pipeline stages and user-perceived performance.
questions.choice_D: Report kernel time without synchronization to avoid overheads.

questions.question: Why can model parallelism complicate throughput measurements?
questions.choice_A: It forces lower precision arithmetic.
questions.choice_B: Inter-device communication and load imbalance can become bottlenecks, making scaling non-linear with the number of devices.
questions.choice_C: It disables caching mechanisms during decoding.
questions.choice_D: It requires per-layer reinitialization each step.

questions.question: Which metric pair most directly characterizes efficiency in combined performance-energy reporting?
questions.choice_A: FLOPs and parameters.
questions.choice_B: Utilization percentage and temperature.
questions.choice_C: Tokens/sec and joules/token, optionally alongside accuracy metrics.
questions.choice_D: Clock speed and memory capacity.

questions.question: In comparative reports across precisions (FP32, FP16, INT8), what should be controlled to make accuracy trade-offs interpretable?
questions.choice_A: Use different datasets per precision to avoid overfitting.
questions.choice_B: Calibrate quantization consistently and evaluate on the same benchmarks to report any accuracy deltas alongside performance gains.
questions.choice_C: Disable KV caching for lower precisions.
questions.choice_D: Scale batch size arbitrarily to match throughput.

questions.question: How should memory footprint be measured to capture realistic peak usage during inference?
questions.choice_A: Record only the model weights size on disk.
questions.choice_B: Use framework-reported current allocation without accounting for fragmentation.
questions.choice_C: Measure peak allocated device memory during a full representative run, including caches, temporary buffers, and fragmentation overhead.
questions.choice_D: Estimate from parameter count times bytes per parameter.

questions.question: What is the correct interpretation of a Pareto frontier when analyzing latency vs. accuracy trade-offs?
questions.choice_A: Models on the frontier have the lowest latency regardless of accuracy.
questions.choice_B: Any point below the frontier is strictly better than those on it.
questions.choice_C: Points on the frontier are not dominated: no other configuration is better in both latency and accuracy simultaneously.
questions.choice_D: The frontier contains only the single fastest and single most accurate models.

questions.question: Which practice improves fairness when comparing throughput across software stacks?
questions.choice_A: Include tokenization time in one system but not the other to reflect real-world usage.
questions.choice_B: Synchronize timing with explicit device barriers and measure identical request mixes, including context lengths and sampling parameters.
questions.choice_C: Choose the fastest batch size for each stack independently without reporting it.
questions.choice_D: Ignore outliers without documenting criteria.

questions.question: What is a robust way to report end-to-end efficiency of an inference service beyond kernel-level metrics?
questions.choice_A: GPU kernel time only.
questions.choice_B: Requests/sec and p95 latency measured at the service boundary, plus tokens/sec and joules/token, under a specified workload and SLO.
questions.choice_C: Average CPU utilization.
questions.choice_D: Model FLOPs per token.
